questions.stem: In a classroom demonstration, for an aluminum system with internal energy change 108 kJ and entropy change -65 J per K held at constant volume, compute the Helmholtz free energy change at 337 K in kJ.

options.misconception: Ignored entropy and reported internal energy alone
Correct application of the principle
Added the T delta S term instead of subtracting
Did not convert entropy units to kJ

questions.explanation: Helmholtz free energy is defined as A equals U minus T S, so its change at constant temperature is delta U minus T delta S. With entropy in J per K converted to kJ per K, the value at 337 K is 129.91 kJ; its decrease sets the maximum work obtainable at constant volume and temperature.
questions.hint: Delta A = delta U - T delta S.

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Maximum Non-Expansion Work principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a worked example, a nickel process at constant temperature and pressure has delta H -77 kJ and delta S -46 J per K at 312 K; find the maximum non-expansion work in kJ.

options.misconception: Used enthalpy change instead of free energy
Used delta G itself instead of its negative
Correct application of the principle
Used the negative of enthalpy instead of free energy

questions.explanation: At constant temperature and pressure the maximum useful non-expansion work equals minus the change in Gibbs free energy. Computing delta G as delta H minus T delta S gives -62.65 kJ, so the maximum non-expansion work is 62.65 kJ; a negative delta G corresponds to positive work available.
questions.hint: Maximum non-PV work = -delta G.

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Otto Cycle Efficiency principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a classroom demonstration, with copper cylinder walls, compression ratio 11, and inlet temperature 298 K, an ideal Otto cycle at gamma 1.4 runs; compute its air-standard thermal efficiency as a percentage.

options.misconception: Used a simple one minus reciprocal ratio expression
Used gamma instead of gamma minus one in the exponent
Reported the reciprocal term without subtracting it
Correct application of the principle

questions.explanation: The ideal Otto efficiency is one minus one over the compression ratio raised to gamma minus one. With compression ratio 11 and gamma 1.4 the exponent is 0.4, giving 61.7 percent; raising the compression ratio increases efficiency but is limited by knock in real engines.
questions.hint: Otto efficiency = 1 - 1/r^(gamma - 1).

questions.learningObjective: Apply Brayton Cycle Efficiency principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a practice exercise, with brass compressor blades, pressure ratio 4, and inlet temperature 300 K, an ideal Brayton cycle at gamma 1.4 runs. Compute its thermal efficiency as a percentage.

options.misconception: Reported the pressure term itself without subtracting
Flipped the sign of the pressure-ratio exponent
Correct application of the principle
Used gamma instead of (gamma minus one) over gamma

questions.explanation: For an ideal Brayton cycle the efficiency depends on the pressure ratio as one minus rp raised to minus (gamma minus one) over gamma. With rp equal to 4 and gamma 1.4 this gives 32.7 percent; higher pressure ratios improve efficiency at the cost of heavier compressors.
questions.hint: Brayton efficiency = 1 - (1/rp)^((gamma-1)/gamma).

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Carnot Cycle Work principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a worked example, a nickel Carnot engine working between 600 K and 370 K absorbs 655 J per cycle from the hot reservoir; calculate the work output per cycle in joules.

options.misconception: Computed the heat rejected rather than the work
Reported the full absorbed heat as work
Added the reservoir ratio to the absorbed heat
Correct application of the principle

questions.explanation: A reversible Carnot engine converts a fraction (1 minus Tc over Th) of the absorbed heat into work. With reservoirs at 600 K and 370 K and heat input 655 J, the work output is 251 J per cycle; the remainder is rejected to the cold reservoir.
questions.hint: Work = Q_in (1 - T_cold/T_hot) for a Carnot cycle.

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Compression-Ignition Cycle Efficiency principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a practice exercise, at compression ratio 19 and cutoff ratio 1.69 with gamma 1.4, an ideal compression-ignition cycle with lead pistons runs. Compute its air-standard efficiency as a percentage.

options.misconception: Correct application of the principle
Used the Otto cycle formula and ignored the cutoff ratio
Reported only the cutoff correction, not one minus it
Used gamma rather than gamma minus one

questions.explanation: The compression-ignition cycle efficiency equals one minus one over r to the gamma minus one times a cutoff-ratio factor (rho to the gamma minus one) over (gamma times rho minus one). With r 19 and rho 1.69 the efficiency is 65.4 percent; at a cutoff ratio of one it reduces to the Otto result.
questions.hint: Diesel-type efficiency = 1 - [1/r^(gamma-1)] [(rho^gamma - 1)/(gamma(rho - 1))].

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Rankine Cycle Efficiency principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a classroom demonstration, a steam Rankine plant with copper piping adds 2362 kJ per kg in the boiler and rejects 716 kJ per kg in the condenser; evaluate the cycle thermal efficiency as a percentage.

options.misconception: Reported the rejected-heat fraction as efficiency
Divided net work by the condenser rejection
Inverted the heat-addition-to-rejection ratio
Correct application of the principle

questions.explanation: Thermal efficiency of any power cycle is net work divided by heat input, which for a Rankine plant is (Qin minus Qout) over Qin. Substituting 2362 and 716 kJ per kg gives 69.7 percent; the condenser rejection is a necessary loss, not part of the useful output.
questions.hint: Efficiency = (Q_boiler - Q_condenser) / Q_boiler.
